title: Furthest Roof with Bricks and Ladders
statement:
A row of rooftops has heights heights[0..n−1]. You start on roof 0 and move right one roof at a time.

Stepping from roof i to roof i + 1 is free when the next roof is the same height or lower. When it is higher by d, you must pay for the climb in one of two ways: spend exactly d bricks, or use up one ladder, which covers any height.

You hold bricks bricks and ladders ladders. Spend them as wisely as you can, and return the largest roof index you can reach.

examples.why: The climbs are 5, 4, 1, 5. Put the ladder on the 5 and all 4 bricks on the 4. The 1-unit climb to roof 4 can't be paid.
Climbs are 5, 2 and 4. Using bricks while they last (5 bricks, then the ladder on the 2) leaves 1 brick for the 4 and stops at roof 3. The ladder belongs on the 5.
Spend the brick on the 1-unit climb and save the ladder for the 8-unit one. Using the ladder first gets stuck at roof 1.

hints: A ladder is worth the most on the tallest climb. But you don't know the tallest climbs ahead of time. What if you could change your mind about past climbs?
Pretend you used a ladder on every climb so far. When you run out of ladders, one past climb has to be paid with bricks instead. Which one is cheapest to switch?

Keep the climbs that currently hold ladders in a min-heap. When the heap is bigger than the number of ladders, pop the smallest climb and pay for it with bricks. The first time bricks go negative, you are stuck on the current roof.

explain.intuition:
Suppose you already know which climbs lie between roof 0 and roof j. You reach j if the ladders cover the ladders biggest climbs and the bricks cover the rest. Any other split costs more bricks.

Walking right, keep the climbs that "hold ladders" in a min-heap. Each new climb goes in. If the heap now holds more climbs than you have ladders, the smallest one in it should be paid with bricks instead, so pop it and subtract it from bricks. The heap always holds the biggest climbs seen so far, so you never spend bricks where a ladder would save more. When bricks go negative, the current roof is as far as you get.
steps: Create an empty min-heap of climb sizes.
For each i from 0 to n − 2, compute d = heights[i + 1] − heights[i]. Skip it if d ≤ 0.
Push d. If the heap size is now larger than ladders, pop the smallest climb and subtract it from bricks.
If bricks < 0, return i: you can't step past roof i.
pitfalls: Spending bricks first and ladders only when bricks run short. In the second example that wastes the ladder on a 2-unit climb.
Using ladders first. In the third example the ladder goes on a 1-unit climb and the 8-unit climb can't be paid.
Returning i + 1 when bricks go negative. The climb onto roof i + 1 is the one you couldn't pay, so you stay on roof i.

solutions.title: Check each roof from scratch
solutions.idea: For every roof j in order, collect the climbs before it, give ladders to the biggest ones and check if bricks cover the rest. Stop at the first roof that fails.

solutions.title: Min-heap of ladder climbs
solutions.idea: Give every climb a ladder for now. When there are more climbs than ladders, move the smallest one to bricks. Stop when bricks go negative.

followups: Solve it with binary search on the answer instead of a heap. What does the check for one candidate roof cost?
Bricks now have a price and ladders have a different price. You must reach the last roof at minimum cost. What changes?
